question: Who is your favourite poet?
answer: My favourite poet is Allama Muhammad Iqbal, because his poetry awakens a sense of hope, self-respect and love for one's homeland. I also admire Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, whose verses carry a message of love and devotion. Discussing my choice with my partner helped me learn why different people admire different poets.
explanation: This is the first pre-reading discussion question; it is meant to be answered orally in pairs before reading the text about Shah Abdul Latif.

question: Share some couplets that you like.
answer: I like the following couplet by Allama Iqbal: 'Khudi ko kar buland itna ke har taqdeer se pehle, Khuda bande se khud poochhe, bata teri raza kya hai' ('Raise yourself so high that before every decree, God Himself asks you, tell Me, what is your wish'). I also like Shah Latif's verse in which he prays, 'My beloved Allah, may you always make Sindh, a land of abundance.' These couplets teach hope, self-belief and love for one's land.
explanation: A pre-reading oral activity that encourages students to recall and share poetry they already know.

question: Do you know the name of any famous Sufi poet of Sindh?
answer: Yes. The most famous Sufi poet of Sindh is Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, who is lovingly called Lal Latif by his devotees. He is considered the greatest Muslim poet of the Sindhi language, and his poetry is collected in the Shah Jo Risalo. Another well-known Sufi figure of Sindh is Shah Inayat, but Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai is by far the best known.
explanation: This pre-reading question activates background knowledge and leads the class towards the main reading text on Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai.

question: How many aspects of Shah Abdul Latif's life have been covered in the text?
answer: Seven aspects of Shah Abdul Latif's life have been covered in the text.
explanation: The reading text is divided into seven numbered sections, each dealing with one aspect of the poet's life: Background and Family, The Name Bhitai, Early Life and Education, Youth, Spiritual Growth, Death and Remembrance, and Shah Latif's Poetry.

question: List all these aspects in your notebook as shown below. (The first aspect is about his Background and Family.)
answer: The first aspect is about his Background and Family. The second aspect is about The Name Bhitai. The third aspect is about his Early Life and Education. The fourth aspect is about his Youth. The fifth aspect is about his Spiritual Growth. The sixth aspect is about his Death and Remembrance. The seventh aspect is about Shah Latif's Poetry.
explanation: Students must list, in order, the seven headings used to organise the reading text on Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai.

question: Those who have an abundance of wealth have ______.
answer: Those who have an abundance of wealth have a lot of wealth.
explanation: 'Abundance' means a very large quantity of something, so having an abundance of wealth means having a lot of wealth.
optionsRaw: (a) little wealth (b) a lot of wealth (c) some wealth

question: My family's ancestral roots are in Sindh, means my parents, grandparents and great grandparents have lived in Sindh since ______.
answer: My family's ancestral roots are in Sindh, means my parents, grandparents and great grandparents have lived in Sindh since many generations.
explanation: 'Ancestral roots' refers to the place from which one's family originally came and where it has lived for many generations.
optionsRaw: (a) my grandparents got married (b) my birth (c) many generations

question: The new academic year commences in our school in April.
answer: The new academic year commences (begins) in our school in April.
explanation: 'Commences' means begins or starts.

question: The devotees of some saints walk to shrines barefoot.
answer: The devotees (followers) of some saints walk to shrines barefoot.
explanation: A devotee is a person who is very devoted to a religion or to a person, that is, a follower.

question: Many people go to a mystic to ask for the fulfilment of their wishes.
answer: Many people go to a mystic (a person with spiritual power) to ask for the fulfilment of their wishes.
explanation: A mystic is a person who seeks direct union with God and is believed to possess spiritual power.
optionsRaw: (a) person who lives alone (b) new person (c) person with spiritual power

question: The sailors of Sindh used to travel to far off lands as they had good navigation skills.
answer: The sailors of Sindh used to travel to far off lands as they had good navigation (ship directing) skills.
explanation: Navigation is the skill of planning and directing the course of a ship or aircraft.

question: For centuries, the main medium for transfer of information was oral traditions.
answer: For centuries, the main medium for transfer of information was oral traditions (passing of information by word of mouth).
explanation: Oral traditions are customs, stories and information handed down from one generation to another by speaking, not by writing.

options.text: passing of information by word of mouth

optionsRaw: (a) horses (b) passing of information by word of mouth (c) messages

question: My brother is a restless person, always looking for new things to do.
answer: My brother is a restless (change seeking) person, always looking for new things to do.
explanation: 'Restless' means unable to stay still or content, always seeking change or new activity.

question: Truly great persons deserve reverence as they play a positive role in our lives.
answer: Truly great persons deserve reverence (respect and admiration) as they play a positive role in our lives.
explanation: 'Reverence' means deep respect and admiration.
optionsRaw: (a) richness and wealth (b) leadership positions (c) respect and admiration

question: Islam's message of peace is universal, as without it there can be no happiness.
answer: Islam's message of peace is universal (applicable to all the people in the world), as without it there can be no happiness.
explanation: 'Universal' means applicable to or shared by all people in the world.

options.text: applicable to all the people in the world

optionsRaw: (a) good (b) applicable to all the people in the world (c) acceptable

question: The ______ of Shah Bhitai celebrate his Urs every year.
answer: The devotees of Shah Bhitai celebrate his Urs every year.
explanation: The bold words of Exercise 2 are to be used once each; a devotee is a devoted follower, so 'devotees' fits here.

question: My mother and I decided to go to a ______ to ask him to pray for my father's health.
answer: My mother and I decided to go to a mystic to ask him to pray for my father's health.
explanation: A mystic is a person with spiritual power to whom people go for prayers and blessings.

question: It is a ______ fact that no living thing can survive without oxygen.
answer: It is a universal fact that no living thing can survive without oxygen.
explanation: 'Universal' means applicable to everyone and everything, so it suits a fact that is true for all living things.

question: Much of what we know about our culture has been passed on to us through ______.
answer: Much of what we know about our culture has been passed on to us through oral traditions.
explanation: Culture is largely handed down by word of mouth, which is described as oral traditions.

question: We may have different ______ but we are all the off springs of Adam.
answer: We may have different ancestral roots but we are all the off springs of Adam.
explanation: 'Ancestral roots' refers to the different origins or families from which people come.

question: Fasting ______ on the first day of Ramadan.
answer: Fasting commences on the first day of Ramadan.
explanation: 'Commences' means begins, which is exactly what fasting does on the first day of Ramadan.

question: Pakistan has everything in ______ but we need strong policies to make good use of everything that we have.
answer: Pakistan has everything in abundance but we need strong policies to make good use of everything that we have.
explanation: 'In abundance' means in large quantities, which is what the sentence requires about Pakistan's resources.

question: Nelson Mandela won his people's ______ for his long struggle for the rights of people in South Asia.
answer: Nelson Mandela won his people's reverence for his long struggle for the rights of people in South Asia.
explanation: 'Reverence' means deep respect and admiration, which a leader earns through long struggle for people's rights.

question: The art of ______ requires hard work and one needs to practise a lot to write beautifully.
answer: The art of calligraphy requires hard work and one needs to practise a lot to write beautifully.
explanation: The blank calls for the art of beautiful writing, that is 'calligraphy'. This word is not printed in the Exercise 2 list, so it has been inferred from the meaning of the sentence; the exercise appears to have a minor gap in its word bank.

question: The Pakistan Navy has very good ______ skills.
answer: The Pakistan Navy has very good navigation skills.
explanation: Navigation is the skill of directing the course of ships, which is a primary skill for a navy.

question: He found pleasure in praying, thinking and devotion. (Write the aspect number.)
answer: 5 (Spiritual Growth).
explanation: The section on Spiritual Growth says that Latif's love of God grew so much that he found pleasure only in devotion and spent most of his time in prayers and deep thinking.

question: He was married for a short period of time only. (Write the aspect number.)
answer: 4 (Youth).
explanation: The section on Youth tells us that Shah Latif married Bibi Saidha Begum in 1713 and his wife died at an early age, so the marriage lasted only a short time.

question: Shah Latif's forefather migrated to Sindh from Afghanistan. (Write the aspect number.)
answer: 1 (Background and Family).
explanation: The section on Background and Family states that Shah Latif's ancestral roots lay in Afghanistan and that his father or ancestors migrated to Sindh.

question: A shrine was built over his grave sometime after his death. (Write the aspect number.)
answer: 6 (Death and Remembrance).
explanation: The section Death and Remembrance says that King Ghulam Shah Kalhoro built a grand mausoleum over his grave after his death.

question: His poetry is mainly about Sindh but off places are also mentioned. (Write the aspect number.)
answer: 7 (Shah Latif's Poetry).
explanation: The section on Shah Latif's Poetry states that he wrote mainly about Sindh and its neighbouring regions but also mentions distant cities such as Istanbul and Samarqand.

question: He loved studying and had a command over other languages. (Write the aspect number.)
answer: 3 (Early Life and Education).
explanation: The section Early Life and Education tells us that although he received little formal education, he knew Arabic and Persian quite well and had in-depth knowledge of the Holy Qur'an and the Hadiths.

question: He is called Bhitai because he spent a good past of his life on a mound. (Write the aspect number.)
answer: 2 (The Name Bhitai).
explanation: This is the example already done in the book: 'bhit' means a mound in Sindhi, and because Shah Latif lived on a mound for the rest of his life he came to be known as Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai.

question: Two things done at the time of 'Urs', as mentioned in the text.
answer: At the time of the Urs, (i) thousands of people gather and listen to the saint's songs sung on the Tambooro, and (ii) many learned men read papers that tell about Latif's life and his poetry.
explanation: The Urs is held at his shrine every year on 14th Safar, the second month of the Muslim calendar, and lasts for three days.

question: Two possible reasons why his ancestors migrated to Sindh.
answer: (i) Shah's father, Syed Habib Shah, migrated from Matyaru in Afghanistan to Bhainpur in Sindh in order to gain spiritual contact with Bilawal, a local pious man; (ii) Sindh was then a centre of Muslim culture and Shah Latif's ancestors liked it so much that they decided to make it their home.
explanation: Some historians give the reason of spiritual contact with Bilawal, while others say that his ancestors migrated to Sindh from Hirat and stayed because they liked the land.

question: Two other languages that he knew quite well.
answer: He knew Arabic and Persian quite well.
explanation: Although he received little formal education, the Risalo provides proof that Shah Latif had a good command of Arabic and Persian.

question: Two main religious sources that he had knowledge about.
answer: He had in-depth knowledge of the Holy Qur'an and the Hadiths.
explanation: References in Shah Jo Risalo indicate his deep familiarity with the Holy Qur'an and the Hadiths.

question: Two poets whose works were a part of his collection.
answer: The Masnavi of Moulana Jalaluddin Rumi and the poems of Shah Karim were part of his poetic collection.
explanation: The text mentions that Shah Latif's poetic collections included the Masnavi of Moulana Jalaluddin Rumi and Shah Karim's poems.

question: Two skills for which he is known.
answer: He is known for (i) the skill of composing poetry (he started composing poetry as a boy and his verses are collected in Shah Jo Risalo), and (ii) his deep knowledge and skill as a Sufi scholar and mystic.
explanation: The text describes him both as a poet of the people and as a Sufi scholar and saint with deep spiritual knowledge.

question: Two places in Afghanistan mentioned in his poetry.
answer: Kabul and Kandahar are the two places in Afghanistan mentioned in his poetry.
explanation: In the translated verse quoted in the text, the poet says, 'Some wander to Rome, to Kabul and Kandahar.'

question: Two places in India mentioned in his poetry.
answer: Delhi and Deccan are the two places in India mentioned in his poetry.
explanation: In the quoted verse the poet says, 'some lie on Delhi, Deccan, thundering over.'

question: Two languages mentioned in which the 'Risalo' has been translated.
answer: The Risalo has been translated into English and Urdu.
explanation: The text states that his collected poems, compiled as Shah Jo Risalo, have been translated into English, Urdu and other languages.

question: How was information about Shah Latif's early life collected? Why was it collected in this manner?
answer: Information about Shah Latif's early life was mostly collected from oral traditions. The renowned Pakistani scholar, educationist and writer Mirza Kalich Beg collected details about his early life from some of the old people living at that time. These people had heard the facts from their fathers and grandfathers, some of whom had seen Shah Latif in person and had even spoken to him. It was collected in this manner because no written records of his early life existed, so the only available source was the memory and word-of-mouth accounts of people who had lived near him.
explanation: This question tests inference: the text is written on the basis of oral traditions, and the reason is the absence of contemporary written records.

question: Why is Shah Latif called the 'Saint of Bhit'?
answer: Shah Latif is called the 'Saint of Bhit' because in 1742 he left his home and went to live on a mound at some distance from his village. A mound of sand is called 'bhit' in Sindhi, and since he lived on this mound for the rest of his life, he came to be known as the Saint of Bhit, Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, or Shah Latif of the Mound.
explanation: The name Bhitai is derived directly from the Sindhi word 'bhit', meaning a mound.

question: Why did Shah Latif not marry again after his wife died?
answer: Shah Latif did not marry again because after his wife Bibi Saidha Begum died at an early age and without children, his heart turned more and more towards religion and devotion. He felt restless and found it difficult to live a normal domestic life, so he devoted himself completely to prayer and deep thinking instead of marrying again.
explanation: The section on Youth explains that his grief and spiritual inclination turned him away from ordinary domestic life.

question: Why did people become Shah Latif's followers?
answer: People became Shah Latif's followers because his spiritual power grew stronger with prayers and devotion. Anyone who came to him was strongly impressed by his gentle ways, so people began to be attracted towards him and his followers increased day by day.
explanation: The section on Spiritual Growth links his growing spiritual power and gentle nature with the increase in his followers.

question: What does Shah Latif's poetry and work tell us about his knowledge and skills?
answer: Shah Latif's poetry and work tell us that he had wide and deep knowledge. Although he received little formal education, he knew Arabic and Persian quite well, had an in-depth knowledge of the Holy Qur'an and the Hadiths, and studied the Masnavi of Moulana Jalaluddin Rumi and the poems of Shah Karim. His poetry mentions distant cities such as Istanbul, Samarqand, China, Rome, Kabul, Kandahar, Delhi and Deccan, and also describes Sindhi sailors, their navigation techniques and their voyages as far as the Malabar coast, Sri Lanka and the island of Java. This shows that he had knowledge of geography, religion, poetry and seafaring, and great poetic skill.
explanation: This question requires pulling together details from the sections on Early Life and Education and Shah Latif's Poetry.

question: Name the places in the text mentioned in Shah Latif's poetry. Why do you think these places have been mentioned by him?
answer: The places mentioned in his poetry are Istanbul, Samarqand, China, Rome, Kabul, Kandahar, Delhi and Deccan; the text also mentions the Sindhi sailors' voyages to the Malabar coast, Sri Lanka and the island of Java. He mentions these places because he was a poet of the people with a wide outlook and knowledge of the world. The verse in which these places appear describes how the rain clouds return again and again, flashing lightning from all sides, and go to Istanbul, the west, China, Samarqand, Rome, Kabul, Kandahar and Delhi. By mentioning so many distant lands, he shows that the blessing of rain and God's mercy reach the whole world, and he uses this to pray that Allah may always make Sindh a land of abundance and make the whole universe prosperous. Thus the places help him connect his love for Sindh with his love for all humanity and for God.
explanation: The verse translated in the text (Sur Sarang, Shah Jo Risalo) is the source for these place names and for the reason why they are mentioned.

question: Why is Shah Latif's key message in his verses acceptable to everyone?
answer: Shah Latif's key message in his verses is acceptable to everyone because his spiritual and mystic poetry carries a message of love. Since love is a universal feeling, his message is universal and acceptable to the entire human race, regardless of religion, region or language. This is why his poetry has been translated into English, Urdu and other languages and is remembered with love and reverence.
explanation: The section on Shah Latif's Poetry states directly that his message of love makes his poetry universal and acceptable to all.

question: Can we put his message into practice in today's world? If 'Yes' how, if 'No' why not?
answer: Yes, we can put his message into practice in today's world. His message of love, devotion, tolerance and kindness can be practised in many ways: we can treat every human being with respect and kindness regardless of faith, race, nationality or social status; we can help the poor and the needy and share with them whatever we have in abundance; we can avoid hatred, violence and selfishness and instead promote peace and harmony in our families, neighbourhoods and country; we can stay devoted to God and to moral values in our daily lives by praying, being honest and being gentle in our dealings. If every individual follows these values, the hatred and conflict in today's world will be reduced and society will become peaceful and prosperous, just as Shah Latif prayed for.
explanation: An open-ended inferential question; the answer draws on Shah Latif's universal message of love and links it to present-day life.

question: Work in groups of six and prepare questions for conducting an interview of scholars who have studied Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, his life and his poetry. Then prepare a role play in which one member becomes an anchor person while the remaining members become scholars in a TV talk show.
answer: Model interview questions for the TV talk show (the anchor asks each of the five 'scholars' two questions): 1. When and where was Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai born, and what was his family background? 2. Why did his ancestors migrate from Afghanistan to Sindh? 3. Why is he called 'Bhitai' or the 'Saint of Bhit'? 4. What kind of education did he receive, and which languages did he know? 5. Tell us about his married life and why he never married again. 6. How did he spend his time at the mound and by the lake? 7. What is Shah Jo Risalo, and why is it so important in Sindhi literature? 8. Which distant places and which Sindhi sailors are mentioned in his poetry? 9. What is the main message of his poetry, and why is it acceptable to people of every faith? 10. How is his Urs celebrated every year at his shrine? Role play outline: One student acts as the anchor and opens the show by welcoming the audience and introducing the topic 'Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai: The Role Model of Sindh'. The anchor then asks two questions to each of the five panellists in turn; each panellist answers briefly in a respectful, scholarly tone, using facts from the reading text. The anchor closes the show by thanking the scholars and summarising Shah Latif's message of love.
explanation: This is a group activity in which students prepare ten questions and perform a TV talk show role play; the model above supplies the questions and the structure of the role play.

question: What are some of the harmful things that people eat, drink or smoke?
answer: Some of the harmful things that people eat, drink or smoke are cigarettes, bidi, sheesha, gutka, paan with tobacco, betel nut (chhaliya), naswar, alcohol, energy drinks, and too much junk food and sugary soft drinks. Many of these contain tobacco, nicotine, tobacco-specific nitrosamines and large amounts of sugar or harmful chemicals, which slowly damage the body. Student's sample answer: 'What do you think, what are some of the harmful things that people eat, drink or smoke? In my opinion, cigarettes, gutka, naswar and soft drinks are the most common harmful things.'
explanation: Part of the Listening and Speaking exercise on asking and answering questions of a social nature; the answer uses the polite question starter 'what do you think'.

question: How does the use of these harmful things affect their physical health?
answer: The use of these harmful things affects physical health very badly. Tobacco and cigarettes cause lung cancer, throat cancer, heart disease, high blood pressure and constant coughing, and they weaken the immune system. Gutka and betel nut damage the teeth, gums and mouth and can cause oral cancer. Alcohol destroys the liver and the kidneys and harms the brain. Junk food and sugary drinks lead to obesity, diabetes and weak bones. A person also becomes addicted, loses appetite and stamina, falls ill again and again and cannot study or work properly. Student's sample answer: 'In your opinion, how does the use of these harmful things affect physical health? In my opinion, they cause cancer, heart disease and diabetes and make a person weak and addicted.'
explanation: This question uses the polite starter 'in your opinion' and requires a factual, social answer about health effects.

question: How does their use affect their relationships with their friends and other people?
answer: The use of these harmful things affects relationships with friends and other people in a very negative way. An addicted person becomes irritable, moody and unreliable, so friends begin to avoid him. Sometimes he starts mixing with bad company and is pushed towards stealing or lying to get money for these things, and this destroys the trust of friends. He may also become rude or aggressive and quarrel over small matters, which spoils good friendships. In this way, addiction slowly cuts a person off from his well-wishers and he is left alone. Student's sample answer: 'According to you, how does their use affect their relationships with their friends and other people? According to me, addiction spoils friendships, causes quarrels and makes a person lose the trust of his friends.'
explanation: This question uses the polite starter 'according to you' and links addiction to social relationships.

question: How does their use affect their family life?
answer: The use of these harmful things affects family life very badly. A large part of the family income is wasted on buying cigarettes, gutka or alcohol, so the family faces poverty and cannot meet its needs for food, education and medicine. The addicted person becomes ill and short-tempered, quarrels with his wife, parents and children, and neglects his duties and responsibilities. Children, seeing such a bad example, may also start these harmful habits. In the end, the whole family suffers from tension, illness and unhappiness. Student's sample answer: 'What do you say, how does their use affect family life? What do you say, these habits waste the family's money, cause quarrels at home and set a bad example for children.'
explanation: This question uses the polite starter 'what do you say' and requires a social answer about the effects on the family.

question: How does the cost of these things affect a person's life style?
answer: The cost of these things affects a person's life style in a harmful way. Cigarettes, gutka and alcohol are expensive, and an addicted person usually spends a large part of his income on them every day. He therefore has less money left for good food, clothes, education of children, proper housing and medical care, so his standard of living falls. To meet this cost he may take loans, sell household items or fall into debt, and in serious cases he may lose his job because he is often ill or absent. Thus, instead of enjoying a healthy and comfortable life, he is forced into a poor and difficult life style. Student's sample answer: 'Can you tell me, how does the cost of these things affect a person's life style? Can you tell me, it leaves him with very little money for food, education and health, so his standard of living goes down.'
explanation: This question uses the polite starter 'can you tell me' and requires an answer about the economic effect of addiction.

question: After all the students in your group have asked all the questions, select one answer for each one of the questions that you would like to share with the class. Decide who will go and present each answer on behalf of the group.
answer: Model group presentation: Question 1 (harmful things) - 'Our group thinks the most harmful things are cigarettes, gutka, naswar and sugary drinks.' Question 2 (physical health) - 'They cause cancer, heart disease and diabetes and make a person weak and addicted.' Question 3 (friendship) - 'Addiction causes irritability and quarrels and destroys the trust of friends.' Question 4 (family life) - 'It wastes the family's money and causes tension, quarrels and unhappiness at home.' Question 5 (life style) - 'It leaves a person with very little money for food, education and health, so his standard of living goes down.' The group decides that one member will present each answer in front of the class, and the group's best answers are shared with all the students.
explanation: This is the presentation stage of the Listening and Speaking exercise; each group selects one answer for each of the five questions and presents it to the class.

question: I ______ swim when I was a child but I ______ swim now.
answer: I couldn't swim when I was a child but I can swim now.
explanation: The first blank refers to the past time, so 'could/couldn't' is used, and the second blank refers to the present, so 'can' is used. (The reverse pair 'could ... can't' is also grammatically possible.)

question: My brother ______ run fast when he was five years old but he ______ run fast now.
answer: My brother couldn't run fast when he was five years old but he can run fast now.
explanation: The past time ('when he was five years old') takes 'couldn't', and the present time ('now') takes 'can'.

question: They ______ come early but they ______ find a bus earlier.
answer: They can come early but they can't find a bus earlier.
explanation: Both clauses refer to present ability and inability, so 'can' and 'can't' are used. The past pair 'could/couldn't' is also acceptable if the situation is understood as past.

question: Nowadays, Sana ______ speak English fluently but she ______ speak so well a year ago.
answer: Nowadays, Sana can speak English fluently but she couldn't speak so well a year ago.
explanation: 'Nowadays' shows present ability, so 'can' is used, while 'a year ago' shows past time, so 'couldn't' is used.

question: Sameer ______ speak several languages when he was young but now he ______ speak only English fluently.
answer: Sameer could speak several languages when he was young but now he can speak only English fluently.
explanation: 'When he was young' refers to the past and takes 'could'; 'now' refers to the present and takes 'can'.

question: Little Shahzain ______ crawl but he still ______ walk.
answer: Little Shahzain can crawl but he still can't walk.
explanation: Both verbs refer to the baby's present abilities and inabilities, so 'can' and 'can't' are used.

question: Sara ______ embroider and stitch clothes but her sister ______.
answer: Sara can embroider and stitch clothes but her sister can't.
explanation: Present ability and inability are expressed with 'can' and 'can't'.

question: We ______ play after completing our homework but we ______ play before that.
answer: We can play after completing our homework but we can't play before that.
explanation: Permission/ability in the present is shown by 'can' and its negative 'can't'.

question: Write about your abilities/ inabilities in the following blanks. (When I was younger/ When I was nine years old: I could ______ / But, I couldn't ______ / Now, I can ______ / However, I can't ______ / When I grow up, I can ______)
answer: When I was nine years old, I could ride a bicycle. But, I couldn't swim in deep water. Now, I can swim well and I can also ride a bicycle quickly. However, I can't drive a car because I am still too young. When I grow up, I can become a famous doctor and serve my country.
explanation: The task uses 'could/couldn't' for past ability and 'can/can't' for present ability, and 'can' for future ability.

question: Now ask two of your class mates what they could/ couldn't do when they were younger, what they can/ can't do now and what they think they can do in the future. Write their responses in your notebook.
answer: Model responses recorded from classmates: Classmate 1 (Ali): 'When I was six years old, I couldn't write my name neatly. Now I can write neatly in both Urdu and English. When I grow up, I can become an engineer.' Classmate 2 (Sana): 'When I was younger, I could sing well but I couldn't draw. Now I can draw simple pictures, but I can't sing in front of a large audience. In the future, I can become a teacher.' The questions asked were: 'What could you do when you were younger?', 'What couldn't you do when you were younger?', 'What can you do now?', 'What can't you do now?' and 'What can you do in the future?'
explanation: This speaking-and-writing task continues the practice of 'can/can't' and 'could/couldn't' in questions and answers.

question: Dialogue A: Using can/ could for ability. Complete the dialogue given below and add at least 10 lines. (Zahra: Can you speak Chinese, Najma? Najma: No, but I can speak Persian. Zahra: Wow! What about you Farah? Farah: I can't ...... but I can ......)
answer: Zahra: Can you speak Chinese, Najma? Najma: No, but I can speak Persian. Zahra: Wow! What about you Farah? Farah: I can't speak Chinese, but I can speak Sindhi and English quite well. Zahra: That is wonderful, Farah. Could you speak English when you were in class five? Farah: No, I couldn't speak English then, but I can speak it fluently now. Zahra: Najma, could you write Urdu when you were younger? Najma: Yes, I could write Urdu, but I couldn't write it neatly. Now I can write it beautifully. Zahra: Can both of you recite poetry? Farah: I can recite a few verses of Shah Latif, but I can't sing them. Najma: I can't recite poetry, but I can sing folk songs. Zahra: That is great. Can you both join the school's language club? Farah: Yes, we can. We can also help other students learn new languages. Najma: We can teach them Sindhi and Persian, and they can teach us Chinese. Zahra: Then let us join today.
explanation: A model dialogue of more than ten lines that uses 'can/can't' for present ability and 'could/couldn't' for past ability.

question: Dialogue B: Using can/ could/ may for permission. Complete the dialogue given below and add at least 10 lines. (Areeb: I have completed my work. Can I play now? Mother: Yes, you can, but come back soon. Areeb: May I take my new ......? Mother: ...... Bilal: ......)
answer: Areeb: I have completed my work. Can I play now? Mother: Yes, you can, but come back soon. Areeb: May I take my new cricket bat with me? Mother: Yes, you may take it, but take care of it. Bilal: May I also go with him, Mother? Mother: You may go, but only after you finish your homework. Bilal: Could I have half an hour to finish it? Mother: Yes, you can have half an hour, but then you must go straight to the ground with Areeb. Areeb: Can we stay out until sunset? Mother: No, you can't stay out so late; you must be home before dark. Areeb: May I take some water with me? Mother: Of course, you may. Bilal: Can we invite our cousin to play with us tomorrow? Mother: You can invite him, but you must also ask your uncle first.
explanation: A model dialogue of more than ten lines using 'can', 'could' and 'may' to ask for and give permission.

question: Why was the twins' father worried?
answer: The twins' father was worried because although Tanveer and Junaid looked exactly alike, they were quite different in nature. Junaid always thought carefully before doing anything, while Tanveer did things without thinking. The father was worried about Tanveer's careless habit and wanted to make him realize that he should think before doing things.
explanation: This question is discussed orally after reading the story 'Two Brothers' to prepare for the narrative writing task.

question: What did he decide to do?
answer: He decided to set up a competition between the two brothers so that Tanveer would realize that he should think before doing things. He told them that he had saved enough money to buy only one bicycle, so the one who would win the competition would get it. The competition was that both brothers would set out right after the morning prayers and walk as far as each could, and return by sunset; the one who managed to complete the task would get the prize.
explanation: The father's plan is the plot device that reveals the importance of thinking before acting.

question: Who won the competition? Why did he win?
answer: Junaid won the competition. He won because he thought about what he should do before setting off. He walked until midday and then turned around to return home, so he reached home well before sunset and completed the task according to the instructions. Tanveer, on the other hand, ran too far and returned late, so he failed.
explanation: Junaid's careful planning and timely return made him the winner, which is the moral of the story.

question: Who lost the competition? Why did he lose?
answer: Tanveer lost the competition. He lost because he sprinted off without thinking and ran to the end of the town and further, wanting to cover a greater distance and win the prize. As he had been running so fast, he became very tired, so his return journey was slower and he reached home long after sunset. Since he had not returned within the time he was supposed to be back, he failed to complete the task according to the instructions.
explanation: Tanveer's haste and overconfidence caused his failure, in contrast to Junaid's careful planning.

question: What lesson do you think Tanveer learnt?
answer: I think Tanveer learnt that one should always think and plan carefully before doing anything, and that haste and overconfidence lead to failure. He also learnt that covering a greater distance is useless if one cannot complete the task within the given time and according to the instructions. From that day he must have realized that wise planning, patience and self-control bring success, while acting without thinking brings loss.
explanation: This question draws out the moral of the story, which is the theme of the narrative essay that follows.

question: Imagine that you are Tanveer's teacher. You wanted him to win but he was not successful. What do you think he should do / not do? Write a narrative essay keeping the following points in mind: Explain the reason for the competition; state what he did and why; describe what his brother did; explain who won the competition and why; identify the mistakes that Tanveer made; express your regret and explain how you would like him to change.
answer:
THE COMPETITION

Tanveer and Junaid were twin brothers in my class. They looked exactly alike, yet their natures were quite different. Junaid always thought carefully before doing anything, while Tanveer did things without thinking. Their father, who was worried about Tanveer's careless habit, decided to teach him a lesson. He announced that he had saved enough money to buy only one bicycle, and that he would give it to the winner of a competition. Both brothers were to set out right after the morning prayers, walk as far as each could, and return by sunset; the one who completed the task would win the bicycle. As their teacher, I understood that the real reason for the competition was to make Tanveer realize that he should think before acting, and I sincerely hoped that he would win.

On the morning of the competition, however, Tanveer made the very mistake his father was trying to cure. As soon as the prayers were over, he sprinted off without a plan, thinking only of covering the greatest distance and reaching home first. He ran to the end of the town and far beyond, proud that he had left Junaid far behind. He wanted the prize so badly that he never once stopped to ask himself whether he could return in time. Junaid, on the other hand, walked calmly until midday. Instead of running far away, he turned back at the right moment, so that he would be able to reach home comfortably before sunset.

By the time Tanveer realized how tired he was, it was too late. Because he had run so fast, his return journey was slow and painful, and he stumbled home long after sunset. Junaid was already there. Tanveer demanded the prize for having run the farthest, but his father explained that he had not returned within the given time, so the prize would go to Junaid, who had completed the task according to the instructions. Junaid therefore won the competition, not because he was stronger, but because he had planned carefully and kept the rules in mind.

Tanveer's mistakes were clear to me: he acted in haste, he was overconfident, he ignored the time limit and he thought only of distance instead of the whole task. I felt sorry for him and I wished I could have helped him win. Yet I also hope that this failure has taught him a lesson he will never forget. I would like him to change his habit of acting without thinking, to plan before he begins any task, to value patience and self-control, and to remember that success belongs to those who think first and act afterwards.
explanation: This is a model narrative essay of more than four paragraphs written in the third person from the point of view of Tanveer's teacher, following all the points listed in the exercise.

question: Work in groups of three. Think of one story related to you or someone you know quite well. Share your stories with each other, select one story and write a narrative essay by following the steps: brainstorm; select a topic; decide why you want to tell that story; select the points/ideas to include; prepare an outline; write the introductory paragraph giving background and purpose; narrate the incident; relate the incident to the purpose; write the concluding paragraph; and edit for organization, grammar, punctuation and paragraphing.
answer:
MODEL STORY: THE DAY I LEARNED TO BE HONEST

Outline: (1) Introduction - background and purpose: my cousin Aamir, an honest shopkeeper, once found a purse; (2) Incident begins - a busy day at the shop, an old woman leaves her purse behind; (3) Complication - the purse contains a large amount of money and Aamir's friend advises him to keep it; (4) Climax - Aamir refuses and searches for the owner; (5) Resolution - he returns the purse and is rewarded with the woman's prayers and the town's respect; (6) Conclusion - honesty is the best policy.

Yesterday my cousin Aamir told me a story that I shall always remember. Aamir, who is only a few years older than me, runs a small general store in our town. I want to tell this story because it taught me, and everyone who heard it, the value of honesty. One busy afternoon, a heavy downpour had filled the shop with customers, and an old woman came in to buy medicine for her grandson.

While Aamir was serving the other customers, the old woman paid for her things and hurried out into the rain. A few minutes later, Aamir noticed a worn leather purse lying beside the counter. He opened it and was shocked to find a large amount of money inside, more than a whole month's profit of his shop. He remembered that the purse belonged to the old woman. Just then his friend Bilal came in and whispered that no one had seen the purse, so Aamir could easily keep the money. Aamir did not listen to him for a second.

He closed his shop at once, even though he would lose business, and ran through the rain towards the old woman's house, which was at the far end of the town. When the breathless old woman saw her purse, she burst into tears, for the money was meant for her grandson's treatment. She blessed Aamir again and again, and the next day the whole town heard how the young shopkeeper had returned the money.

That day I learnt an important lesson. Aamir's honesty, courage and kindness brought him far more than money; they brought him respect and the heartfelt prayers of a poor woman. From then on, I decided that I would always choose honesty, even when nobody is watching, because honesty is truly the best policy.
explanation: This is a model narrative essay following every step listed in the exercise: brainstorming, topic selection, purpose, outline, introduction, narration, linking the incident to the purpose and a conclusion.

question: Read the following passage about Moen-jo-Daro and underline the main ideas / words in each paragraph; do not include any details. (The first paragraph has been done as an example.)
answer:
Paragraph 1 (example, already done): Moen-jo-Daro or the 'Mound of the Dead' is one of the oldest cities in the world, and it was one of the largest city-settlements of the Indus Valley Civilization of South Asia.

Paragraph 2 (main ideas to be underlined): Nobody knew anything about Moen-jo-Daro until 1922, when villagers found pieces of old smooth pots and old bricks; these were brought to Sir John Marshall, who recognized them as pieces of very old pots and decided that the area should be dug up as there might be remains of an old city.

Paragraph 3 (main ideas to be underlined): The men started digging and, bit by bit, a city of straight roads and well-built houses came up from what had been taken for mounds of clay and sand; each house was made of large baked bricks and had a bathroom and servant quarters, with covered drains beside streets of baked bricks, and a wide road with shops on both sides in the middle.

Paragraph 4 (main ideas to be underlined): The people must have been great traders, with the river Indus near and the sea within easy reach; the countryside was fertile with wheat, rice and cotton, the farmers kept cattle, and there were skilled craftsmen who made things from gold, silver and ivory.

Paragraph 5 (main ideas to be underlined): For a long time these people lived a happy, rich life and travelled from place to place for business or pleasure; their city was well-planned and clean, but we do not know what happened to them - either they were raided from the north or a great earthquake destroyed them.
explanation: The exercise trains students to identify only the main ideas of each paragraph (not details) so that these key words can be used to write a summary in Exercise 5.

question: Use the underlined key words and write a summary of the above passage about Moen-jo-Daro. Look at the Do's and Don'ts given in the boxes above. (You may begin like this: 'Moen-jo-Daro, in Sindh, was one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilization...')
answer: Moen-jo-Daro, in Sindh, was one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilization. This civilization developed around 3000 BC in areas that today form Pakistan and North India, and Moen-jo-Daro, one of the oldest cities in the world, was built around 2600 BC. Nothing was known about it until 1922, when villagers found pieces of old pots and bricks and brought them to Sir John Marshall, who decided that the area should be dug up. When digging began, a well-planned city of straight roads and strong houses of baked bricks appeared, with bathrooms, covered drains and a wide road with shops on both sides. Its people must have been great traders, for the Indus was near and the sea was within easy reach; the fertile land produced wheat, rice and cotton, and skilled craftsmen worked in gold, silver and ivory. For a long time these people lived a happy and rich life, but we do not know what happened to them, for they may have been raided from the north or destroyed by a great earthquake.
explanation: A model summary written from the underlined main ideas of the passage, using simple short sentences and linking words, without reproducing sentences from the original or adding new ideas.

question: Editing Practice (C-test): Beginning from the second word of the second sentence, half or half plus one extra letters have been removed from every second word. Complete all the words and write the complete passage 'The Duties of a Good Citizen' in your notebook.
answer:
THE DUTIES OF A GOOD CITIZEN

If we just think for a minute, about the things and services we use in one day, we shall realize how much we owe to society. The milkman brings milk for us; the baker bakes the bread; the printer prints our books; the driver drives the bus in which we go to school or the place of our work. The teacher teaches the pupils at school, the doctor treats the sick and the shopkeeper sells articles of daily use. The traffic police regulate the traffic so that we may travel without any fear of accident.

We must repay society for all these gifts. If a milkman mixes water in the milk, how can he expect other members of society to treat him fairly? If a shopkeeper gives short measure or sells sub-standard goods, he must be prepared to get the same kind of treatment from others. If we ignore traffic rules, we not only endanger the lives of others but our own as well.

Many benefits we enjoy are provided by our own country and society. It is, therefore, our duty to be loyal and patriotic to Pakistan. We should pay our taxes promptly, fully and honestly, so that we may continue to enjoy all social benefits.

Islam lays great stress on our duties as citizens. The Holy Prophet (peace be upon him) once said, 'God lays so much stress on the rights of our neighbours that I almost thought they would get the right of inheritance in our property.' In short, we cannot be good Muslims without being good and dutiful citizens.
explanation: This is the complete reconstructed passage for the C-test; the missing halves of words are supplied from the context of each sentence.

question: You are the editor of your school magazine. Work in pairs to edit the following passage for the school magazine.
answer:
CORRECTED PASSAGE

Students have mainly three basic duties. They must obey their parents, teachers and elders. Students must help their parents in simple home chores. They must not become unresponsive to parents or teachers.

Students must follow the standard discipline. They must establish a routine of studying. They must learn and practise good manners and habits. They must focus on their studies. Regular reading should be a part of their daily routine, and this reading habit makes them more intelligent and knowledgeable; moreover, it also improves their overall language skills and vocabulary. Besides studying, they must exercise daily. They must avoid watching too much TV. They must be polite and respectful towards everyone. They must eat healthy food and avoid eating food that is unhealthy.

LIST OF CORRECTIONS: 'there parent' corrected to 'their parents'; 'they must not became' corrected to 'They must not become'; 'must fellow' corrected to 'must follow'; 'practice' (verb) corrected to 'practise'; 'routine with studying' corrected to 'routine of studying'; 'Besides study' corrected to 'Besides studying'; 'They avoid watching' corrected to 'They must avoid watching'; 'languach' corrected to 'language'; 'every one' corrected to 'everyone'; 'eating good that is unhealthy' corrected to 'eating food that is unhealthy'.
explanation: The task is to edit the passage for grammar, spelling and punctuation errors (pronouns, verb forms, capitalisation, spelling and word choice) before printing it in the school magazine.

question: Here is one of Shah Latif's poems, 'Rain', translated by Elsa Kazi. Work in groups of four and recite it. Each group should read one verse only.
answer: The poem 'RAIN' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Elsa Kazi, has four verses, and each of the four members of the group recites one verse. Verse 1 (first member): 'The rain pours on the desert sands / On hills and vales around; / At early dawn we rise to hear, / The churns soft, humming sound-'. Verse 2 (second member): 'The hands are full of butter, wives / With merriment abound- / Each buffalo for milking brought; / Athwart the grassy ground; / In thatches here we never found / Mistress and mind so glad!'. Verse 3 (third member): 'Season's Orchestra's in full swing, / Fresh showers ease the mind; / On mountain-side so green with grass; / Cattle abundance find; / Gay herdsmen's wives about their necks / Of blossoms garlands wind;'. Verse 4 (fourth member): 'Cucumbers, mushrooms, vegetables / Food of every kind; / Lord! Days of dearth let lie behind, / Ne'er let them reach the earth.' For good recitation each member should speak clearly and slowly, pause correctly at the commas, and use a soft, happy tone for the joyful scenes and a prayerful tone for the last two lines. The poem describes the joy of the first rain in Sindh: the sound of churning butter, the herdsmen's happy wives, the green mountain-side and the abundance of food, and it ends with a prayer that days of scarcity should never come again.
explanation: The Fun section poem is not to be formally assessed; the model answer gives the four verses with their group divisions and guidance on tone and expression for recitation.

question: Continue working in the same groups of four and draw the scene described in the verse that you recited, on a chart paper. Colour or paint the picture. Write the verse in beautiful and fancy writing on the chart. All the charts will be displayed in the class and the group with the best drawing will be the winner.
answer: For Verse 1, draw rolling desert sands and hills with heavy slanting lines of falling rain, a dark grey sky with flashes of lightning, and a small Sindhi village in the foreground where people stand at dawn listening to the soft humming of the churning pots. For Verse 2, draw a grassy ground with buffaloes being brought for milking, women with hands full of butter and happy smiling faces, and simple thatched huts behind them. For Verse 3, draw a green mountain-side covered with fresh grass, colourful wild flowers, cattle grazing in abundance, and the herdsmen's wives wearing garlands of blossoms around their necks. For Verse 4, draw baskets full of cucumbers, mushrooms and vegetables of every kind, with farmers thanking God, and use bright fresh colours. On each chart, write the verse neatly in fancy lettering using a good pen or marker, add a small border of raindrops or flowers, and write the poet's name (Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai) and the translator's name (Elsa Kazi) at the bottom so that all the charts can be displayed in the class and judged.
explanation: The drawing-and-display activity is only for fun and is not formally assessed; the model answer describes exactly what each group should draw and write for its chosen verse.
